messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Layla is a thirty-year-old divorced woman of Lebanese descent who works as a bartender at a busy downtown cocktail bar. She presented for therapy with a PCL-5 score of 61, describing years of escalating anxiety, hypervigilance, and a growing sense that her world was becoming smaller and less navigable. Her presenting difficulties trace their roots to a childhood saturated with domestic violence — not as a single incident, but as a recurring, unpredictable atmosphere in which her father's rages could erupt without warning. What she remembers most viscerally is not any one night but a quality of motion: the way his arm would rise before the blow, the way her mother's body would flinch and contract, the way a door slamming could precede everything terrible. These were the textures of danger in her childhood home, and they have never fully released her.

Layla cannot tell this story in a straightforward way. When asked to describe what she witnessed, she finds herself arriving at the edge of something she cannot cross into language. She knows what happened — the knowledge sits in her body, in her chest, in the way her hands grip things — but the words dissolve before she can form them. The memories do not arrive as narrative; they arrive as sensation, as a sudden and overwhelming flood of emotion that forces her to stop, to look away, to leave the room. This nonverbal, emotionally saturating quality of the memories means that the past has never been processed into something she can hold at a distance. Instead it remains close, raw, and unresolved — and that unresolved quality has quietly shaped everything she believes about herself and others. She has come to understand herself as someone who cannot be relied upon, who will not do the right thing when it matters, and she has extended this distrust outward: people, in her experience, are not safe. These convictions — that she is unreliable, that others are dangerous — keep the threat of harm feeling perpetually present, as though the violence of her childhood is still occurring somewhere just out of sight.

This sense of ongoing threat is sharpest in her body's response to movement. At the bar where she works, a patron reaching suddenly across the counter, a colleague turning quickly in the narrow space behind the taps — any abrupt movement by another person puts her immediately on guard, her nervous system reading it as the prelude to something she has to survive. She has quietly rearranged her working habits to keep her back to the wall when possible and to monitor the room constantly. Outside of work, she has narrowed her world considerably: open or exposed spaces feel unbearable, as though visibility means vulnerability, and she has stopped walking to her car through the parking structure alone. She checks the locks on her apartment door multiple times each night before she can attempt sleep, and even then she does not feel safe except in the one corner of her apartment she has come to think of as hers.

To manage the threat she feels everywhere, Layla has developed a set of strategies that feel protective but have become their own burden. She rehearses worst-case scenarios in careful, detailed loops — imagining what could go wrong, how she would respond, what she would do if someone hurt her — convinced that preparation is the only thing standing between her and catastrophe. She works hard to suppress whatever emotion surfaces, believing that visible distress would expose her to further harm or judgment. But these strategies, rather than quieting the threat, keep her nervous system in a state of constant activation: the mental rehearsal of catastrophe refreshes the sense of danger rather than resolving it, and the emotional suppression prevents the kind of processing that might allow memories to settle. The rehearsal and suppression cycle back into her appraisals of herself — she interprets the fact that she still feels this afraid as further evidence that she cannot trust herself, that she is fundamentally inadequate to her own life.

What finally brought Layla to seek help was a panic response at work so severe that she had to leave her shift early — something she had never done before, and which her manager noticed. She is afraid, coming into therapy, that she will be unable to speak about what happened. What she hopes for, tentatively and almost without believing it possible, is to one day feel safe somewhere other than her single corner of a locked apartment.
